claim: Self-cleaving ribozymes in the human genome are few and poorly studied.
source: Despite their importance in a wide range of living organisms, self-cleaving ribozymes in the human genome are few and poorly studied.
evidence: This is a statement made in the abstract about the current state of knowledge regarding human self-cleaving ribozymes.

claim: The essential regions of LINE-1 and OR4K15 ribozymes consist of 35 and 31 nucleotides, respectively.
source: We found that the regions essential for ribozyme activities are made of two short segments, with a total of 35 and 31 nucleotides only.
evidence: This claim is supported by deep mutational scanning experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: LINE-1 and OR4K15 ribozymes are the simplest known self-cleaving ribozymes.
source: The discovery makes them the simplest known self-cleaving ribozymes.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the small size of the essential regions identified through experimental data.

claim: The two self-cleaving ribozymes are circular permutations of each other with two nearly identical catalytic internal loops.
source: Moreover, the essential regions are circular permutated with two nearly identical catalytic internal loops, supported by two stems of different lengths.
evidence: This structural relationship is determined from deep mutational scanning and CODA analysis.

claim: LINE-1 and OR4K15 ribozymes are similar to twister sister ribozymes in terms of sequence and secondary structure.
source: These two self-cleaving ribozymes, which are shaped like lanterns, are similar to the catalytic regions of the twister sister ribozymes in terms of sequence and secondary structure.
evidence: This similarity is established through sequence comparison and structural analysis.

claim: Mutational effects on TS-like ribozymes differ from those on twister sister ribozymes at the cleavage site.
source: However, the nucleotides at the cleavage site have shown that mutational effects on two twister sister-like (TS-like) ribozymes are different from the twister sister ribozyme.
evidence: This is demonstrated through mutational analysis comparing the responses of different ribozymes.

claim: TS-like ribozymes represent a ribozyme class with the simplest and perhaps most primitive structure needed for self-cleavage.
source: The discovery of TS-like ribozymes reveals a ribozyme class with the simplest and, perhaps, the most primitive structure needed for self-cleavage.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the minimal size and structural simplicity of the ribozymes.

claim: Ribozymes are thought to have dominated early life forms.
source: Ribozymes (catalytic RNAs) are thought to have dominated early life forms (Benner et al., 1989) until they were gradually replaced by more effective and stable proteins.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Self-cleaving ribozymes are found in a wide range of living organisms.
source: One of the few that remain active is self-cleaving ribozymes found in a wide range of living organisms (Ferré-D'Amaré and Scott, 2010)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Self-cleaving ribozymes are involved in rolling circle replication of RNA genomes.
source: One of the few that remain active is self-cleaving ribozymes found in a wide range of living organisms (Ferré-D'Amaré and Scott, 2010), involved in rolling circle replication of RNA genomes (Forster and Symons, 1987; Hutchins et al., 1986; Prody et al., 1986)
evidence: This functional role is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Self-cleaving ribozymes are involved in biogenesis of mRNA and circRNA.
source: involved in rolling circle replication of RNA genomes (Forster and Symons, 1987; Hutchins et al., 1986; Prody et al., 1986), biogenesis of mRNA and circRNA, gene regulation (Cervera and de la Peña, 2020; de la Peña and García-Robles, 2010a; de la Peña and García-Robles, 2010a; Martick et al., 2008; Salehi-Ashtiani et al., 2006)
evidence: This functional role is supported by citations.

claim: Self-cleaving ribozymes are involved in gene regulation.
source: biogenesis of mRNA and circRNA, gene regulation (Cervera and de la Peña, 2020; de la Peña and García-Robles, 2010a; de la Peña and García-Robles, 2010a; Martick et al., 2008; Salehi-Ashtiani et al., 2006)
evidence: This functional role is supported by citations.

claim: Self-cleaving ribozymes are involved in co-transcriptional scission of retrotransposons.
source: and co-transcriptional scission of retrotransposons (Eickbush and Eickbush, 2010; Sánchez-Luque et al., 2011).
evidence: This functional role is supported by citations.

claim: Two hammerhead ribozymes have been found in the human genome.
source: They include two hammerhead ribozymes (de la Peña and García-Robles, 2010a; Perreault et al., 2011)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: An HDV-like CPEB3 ribozyme exists within the transcript of a single-copy gene in the human genome.
source: an hepatitis delta virus (HDV)-like cytoplasmic polyadenylation element-binding protein 3 (CPEB3) ribozyme within the transcript of a single-copy gene (Salehi-Ashtiani et al., 2006)
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Self-cleaving ribozymes associated with OR4K15, IGF1R, and LINE-1 have been found in the human genome.
source: and self-cleaving ribozymes associated with olfactory receptor OR4K15 (olfactory receptor family 4 subfamily K member 15), insulin-like growth factor 1 receptor (IGF1R), and a LINE-1 (Long Interspersed Nuclear Element-1) retrotransposon (Salehi-Ashtiani et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Human self-cleaving ribozymes were discovered using selection-based biochemical experiments.
source: All these ribozymes were discovered by using selection-based biochemical experiments (Salehi-Ashtiani et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the discovery study.

claim: The hovlinc ribozyme was identified by genome-wide screening for RNAs with specific 5′-hydroxyl termini.
source: More recently, the hovlinc ribozyme (Chen et al., 2021) was identified by genome-wide screening against RNAs with the specific 5′-hydroxyl termini resulted from self-cleavage, followed by a combination of RNA structure prediction as well as deletion analysis and mutation-based validation for determining its secondary structure.
evidence: This is supported by citation to the discovery study.

claim: Single-nucleotide polymorphism in CPEB3 ribozyme is associated with enhanced self-cleavage activity and poorer episodic memory.
source: It has been shown that single-nucleotide polymorphism in CPEB3 ribozyme was associated with an enhanced self-cleavage activity along with a poorer episodic memory (Vogler et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Inhibition of CPEB3 ribozyme can strengthen hippocampal-dependent long-term memory.
source: Inhibition of the highly conserved CPEB3 ribozyme could strengthen hippocampal-dependent long-term memory (Bendixsen et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Little is known about human self-cleaving ribozymes other than CPEB3.
source: However, little is known about the other human self-cleaving ribozymes.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Self-cleaving ribozymes in retrotransposons are important for genome size, structure, and function.
source: Previous studies on self-cleaving ribozymes found in retrotransposons suggested their importance in the overall size, structure, and function of different genomes.
evidence: This is based on previous studies in the field.

claim: Twister ribozyme variants are found in non-LTR retrotransposons of Schistosoma mansoni.
source: Most self-cleaving ribozymes found in retrotransposons belong to three widespread ribozyme families: twister ribozyme variants in non-LTR retrotransposons of Schistosoma mansoni (Liu et al., 2021)
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: HDV-like ribozymes are found in R2 elements.
source: HDV-like ribozymes in R2 elements (Eickbush and Eickbush, 2010)
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: HDV-like ribozymes are found in L1Tc retrotransposon.
source: and L1Tc retrotransposon (Sánchez-Luque et al., 2011)
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Hammerhead ribozymes are found in short interspersed nuclear elements of Schistosomes.
source: and hammerhead ribozymes in short interspersed nuclear elements of Schistosomes (Ferbeyre et al., 1998)
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Hammerhead ribozymes are found in Penelope-like elements.
source: Penelope-like elements (Cervera and De la Peña, 2014; Lünse et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Hammerhead ribozymes are found in retrozymes.
source: and retrozymes (Cervera et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: HDV-like ribozymes usually locate in the 5′ UTR region of retrotransposons only.
source: Unlike the wide occurrence of hammerhead ribozymes in different types of retrotransposons, HDV-like ribozymes usually locate in the 5′ UTR region of the retrotransposons only
evidence: This is a general observation about the distribution of HDV-like ribozymes.

claim: HDV-like ribozymes have been found in different species including Drosophila melanogaster, Bombyx mori, arthropods, nematodes, birds, and tunicates.
source: and were found in different species including Drosophila melanogaster (Dawid and Rebbert, 1981; Roiha et al., 1981), Bombyx mori (Eickbush and Robins, 1985), arthropods, nematodes, birds, and tunicates (Ruminski et al., 2011; Webb et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: HDV-like ribozymes in retrotransposons are important for co-transcriptional processing of the full-length transcript and translation of the downstream open reading frame.
source: These ribozymes are important for co-transcriptional processing of the full-length transcript and translation of the downstream open reading frame.
evidence: This is based on previous studies of HDV-like ribozymes in retrotransposons.

claim: The LINE-1 ribozyme may play an active role in co-transcriptional processing during evolution.
source: This suggests that the LINE-1 ribozyme found in the human genome may also play an active role in co-transcriptional processing during evolution.
evidence: This is an inference based on the similarity to other HDV-like ribozymes in retrotransposons.

claim: Self-cleaving ribozymes are typically in non-coding regions of the genome.
source: Typically, self-cleaving ribozymes are in non-coding regions of the genome.
evidence: This is a general observation about the genomic location of self-cleaving ribozymes.

claim: The CPEB3 ribozyme is located inside the intron of the CPEB3 gene.
source: For example, the CPEB3 ribozyme is located inside the intron of the CPEB3 gene (Salehi-Ashtiani et al., 2006)
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Hammerhead ribozyme is found in the 3′ UTR of Clec2 genes.
source: hammerhead ribozyme found in the 3′ UTR of Clec2 genes (Martick et al., 2008)
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Hammerhead and HDV motifs are associated with retrotransposable elements.
source: hammerhead and HDV motifs associated with retrotransposable elements (Cervera et al., 2016; Ruminski et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The OR4K15 ribozyme is located at the reverse strand of the coding region of the olfactory receptor gene OR4K15.
source: However, the OR4K15 ribozyme is located at the reverse strand of the coding region of the olfactory receptor gene OR4K15, suggesting a potentially novel functional mechanism for this ribozyme.
evidence: This is a finding from the study regarding the genomic location of OR4K15 ribozyme.

claim: Deep mutational scanning combined with CODA analysis can lead to highly accurate inference of base-pairing structures.
source: Our previous work indicates that deep mutational scanning can lead to covariation signals for highly accurate inference of base-pairing structures (Zhang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: LINE-1-ori and OR4K15-ori sequences were generated from randomly fragmented human genomic DNA selection-based biochemical experiments.
source: These original sequences were generated from a randomly fragmented human genomic DNA selection-based biochemical experiments (Salehi-Ashtiani et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the original discovery study.

claim: There is no exact match for LINE-1-ori and OR4K15-ori in the human genome.
source: It needs to be noted that there is no exact match for LINE-1-ori and OR4K15-ori in the human genome (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by genomic location analysis shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The lack of exact matches for LINE-1-ori and OR4K15-ori in the human genome is related to mutations accumulated during selection.
source: This should be related to mutations accumulated during the selection.
evidence: This is an inference about why the original sequences don't match the genome exactly.

claim: Mutations in most positions in LINE-1-ori do not lead to large changes in relative activity.
source: Mutations in most positions in LINE-1-ori did not lead to large changes in RA.
evidence: This is based on deep mutational scanning data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The activity of LINE-1-ori ribozyme is only sensitive to mutations in two short segments (54–71 and 83–99).
source: The activity of the LINE-1-ori ribozyme is only sensitive to the mutations in two short segments (54–71 and 83–99) where the RA can be reduced to nearly zero.
evidence: This is based on deep mutational scanning data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The two terminal ends and the central region between bases 72 and 82 of LINE-1-ori are not important for self-cleavage activity.
source: Thus, the two terminal ends and the central region between bases 72 and 82 are not that important for LINE-1 self-cleavage activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the mutational sensitivity data.

claim: Only sequence positions inside two short segments (70–84 and 101–116) of OR4K15-ori are sensitive to mutations.
source: Only sequence positions inside the two short segments (70–84 and 101–116) are sensitive to mutations, which suggests that only these regions are required to form the functional RNA structure of the OR4K15 self-cleaving ribozyme.
evidence: This is based on deep mutational scanning data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The contiguous functional region of LINE-1 ribozyme is 54–99 (LINE-1-rbz).
source: Thus, we have identified the contiguous functional regions of LINE-1 ribozymes (54–99, LINE-1-rbz)
evidence: This is determined from deep mutational scanning data.

claim: The contiguous functional region of OR4K15 ribozyme is 70–116 (OR4K15-rbz).
source: and OR4K15 ribozymes (70–116, OR4K15-rbz).
evidence: This is determined from deep mutational scanning data.

claim: CODA analysis of LINE-1-ori reveals four base pairs in one stem region and two base pairs in a second stem region.
source: The CODA result for LINE-1-ori shows four base pairs (A14U34, A16U32, G17C31, C18G30) in one possible stem region, and another two base pairs (A4U43, A6A41) in the second possible stem region.
evidence: This is based on CODA analysis of deep mutational scanning data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: CODA analysis of OR4K15-ori shows fewer base pairs than LINE-1-ori due to lower mutational coverage.
source: Due to the lower mutational coverage, the CODA result for OR4K15-ori shows fewer base pairs than LINE-1-ori.
evidence: This is based on CODA analysis of deep mutational scanning data.

claim: Low mutation coverage for OR4K15-ori was due to mutational bias of error-prone PCR.
source: The low mutation coverage for OR4K15-ori was due to the mutational bias (Cadwell and Joyce, 1992; Keohavong and Thilly, 1989) of error-prone PCR (Figure 1—figure supplements 1–4).
evidence: This is based on analysis of mutation patterns and supported by citations about error-prone PCR biases.

claim: LINE-1-rbz has two highly reliable stem regions with a length of 6 nt, including one non-Watson–Crick pair A6A41.
source: LINE-1-rbz has two highly reliable stem regions with a length of 6 nt, including one non-Watson–Crick pair A6A41.
evidence: This is based on CODA+MC analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: OR4K15-rbz has two reliable stem regions with lengths of 5 nt and 4 nt, including one non-Watson–Crick pair G14U33.
source: For OR4K15-rbz, the functional region has two reliable stem regions with lengths of 5 nt and 4 nt, respectively, including one non-Watson–Crick pair G14U33.
evidence: This is based on CODA+MC analysis shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Most base pairs discovered by MC simulated annealing are non-AU pairs.
source: Most of the base pairs discovered by MC simulated annealing are non-AU pairs, whose covariations are difficult to capture by error-prone PCR because of mutational biases (Cadwell and Joyce, 1992; Keohavong and Thilly, 1989).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the CODA+MC results and supported by citations about PCR biases.

claim: The two stems identified are consistent with the single mutation profiles.
source: In addition, these two stems are consistent with the single mutation profiles.
evidence: This is based on comparison of structural predictions with mutational data.

claim: G14A and U33C single mutations in OR4K15-rbz show high relative activity (1.55 and 1.82, respectively).
source: For example, two single mutations G14A and U33C showed high RA, 1.55 and 1.82, respectively
evidence: This is based on deep mutational scanning data.

claim: G14A and U33C mutations change the wobble GU pair to Watson–Crick AU and GC pairs, leading to more stable structure and higher activity.
source: suggesting the high possibility of a G14U33 pair at these positions, because these two separate mutations change the wobble GU pair to the Watson–Crick AU and GC pairs, respectively, and lead to a more stable structure and higher activity.
evidence: This is an inference based on mutational data and knowledge of base-pairing stability.

claim: The second round of deep mutational scanning of LINE-1-rbz achieved 99.3% and 99.9% coverage of single and double mutations, respectively.
source: More importantly, it achieves 99.3% and 99.9% coverage of single and double mutations, respectively, within the contiguous functional segment (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the sequencing data from the second round of deep mutational scanning.

claim: The first round of deep mutational scanning of LINE-1-ori had only 18.5% coverage of double mutations.
source: Performing the second round was necessary because the deep mutational scanning of the original LINE-1 ribozyme had a low 18.5% coverage of double mutations (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the sequencing data from the first round.

claim: RtcB ligase selectively captures cleaved RNAs because it only reacts with 5′-hydroxyl termini that exist only in cleaved RNAs.
source: In addition, to amplify the signals of cleaved RNAs after in vitro transcription of the mutant library of LINE-1-rbz, we selectively captured cleaved RNAs by employing RtcB ligase and a 5′-desbiotin, 3′-phosphate modified linker because they only react with the 5′-hydroxyl termini that exist only in cleaved RNAs (Tanaka et al., 2011).
evidence: This is based on the known specificity of RtcB ligase supported by citation.

claim: The chemically synthesized doped library with 6% doping rate leads to less biased mutations compared to error-prone PCR.
source: The technology improvement leads to less biased mutations in terms of the sequence positions (Figure 1—figure supplements 1 and 2) and mutation types (Figure 1—figure supplements 3 and 4).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparison of mutation patterns shown in supplementary figures.

claim: RA′ is a good estimate of RA with a Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.66 and Spearman correlation coefficient of 0.769.
source: We confirmed RA′ as a good estimate of RA by comparing shared single mutations from LINE-1-ori and LINE-1-rbz and obtained a strong Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.66 (Spearman correlation coefficient of 0.769).
evidence: This is based on statistical comparison of the two measures.

claim: Moderate or high relative activity values (RA′ > 0.5) at the two outer ends of the stem regions suggest these nucleotides might not be necessary for LINE-1-rbz function.
source: Moderate or high relative activity values (RA′ > 0.5) at the two outer ends (18C, 30G, C46) of the stem regions suggest that these nucleotides might not be necessary for the function of LINE-1-rbz
evidence: This is inferred from the mutational data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Data from both the original sequence and functional region of LINE-1 ribozyme reveal the existence of two stem regions.
source: Figure 2B shows that data from both the original sequence and functional region of the ribozyme reveal the existence of two stem regions.
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparison of CODA results shown in Figure 2B.

claim: LINE-1-rbz CODA analysis clearly shows two stems with lengths of 6 nt and 5 nt due to nearly 100% coverage of single and double mutations.
source: The latter clearly shows two stems with lengths of 6 nt and 5 nt, respectively, due to nearly 100% coverage of single and double mutations for the functional region.
evidence: This is based on CODA analysis with high mutation coverage.

claim: CODA analysis suggests a non-canonical pair 6A41A at the end of the first stem of LINE-1-rbz, though the signal is weak.
source: Moreover, it suggests a non-canonical pair 6A41A at the end of the first stem, although the signal is weak.
evidence: This is based on CODA analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Weak covariation signals for non-canonical pairs are expected because they are typically less stable than standard base pairings.
source: Such a weak signal is expected because the non-canonical pairs are typically less stable than standard base pairings (Lemieux and Major, 2002).
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about non-canonical base pairs supported by citation.

claim: CODA+MC removed mostly local false positives from the probabilistic CODA results.
source: The resulting base pairs (Figure 2C, upper triangle) removed mostly local false positives.
evidence: This is based on comparison of CODA and CODA+MC results shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The non-canonical AA pair was removed by CODA+MC likely because the energy function does not account for non-canonical pairs.
source: However, the non-canonical AA pair was removed as well, likely because the energy function does not account for non-canonical pairs.
evidence: This is an inference about why CODA+MC removed a potentially true base pair.

claim: A new 18C30G pair added by CODA+MC is a natural extension of the second stem.
source: A new 18C30G pair added is a natural extension of the second stem.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of the CODA+MC results.

claim: Two consecutive base pairs (7G37C, 8C36G) added by CODA+MC are likely false positives because they appear with low probability (0.52).
source: Two separate consecutive base pairs (7G37C, 8C36G) with relatively low signals were also added in the CODA+MC result. These two base pairs are likely false positives because they do not appear in all the models generated from MC simulated annealing with a low probability of 0.52.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the MC simulated annealing results.

claim: LINE-1-rbz ribozyme contains two stem regions (P1, P2), two internal loops, and a stem-loop.
source: Taking all the information together leads to a confident secondary structure for the LINE-1-rbz ribozyme, which contains two stem regions (P1, P2), two internal loops, and a stem-loop (Figure 2D, left).
evidence: This is the final secondary structure model based on all the data, shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The secondary structures of LINE-1-rbz and OR4K15-rbz are surprisingly similar to each other.
source: The secondary structures for these two ribozymes (Figure 2D) are surprisingly similar to each other.
evidence: This is based on comparison of the structures shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Both LINE-1-rbz and OR4K15-rbz have two stems (P1, P2), two internal loops and a stem-loop region.
source: Both ribozymes have two stems (P1, P2), two internal loops and a stem-loop region.
evidence: This is based on the secondary structure models shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Both stem-loop regions (SL2) of LINE-1-rbz and OR4K15-rbz are insensitive to mutations.
source: Both stem-loop regions (SL2) are insensitive of ribozyme activity to mutations (Figure 1B, C).
evidence: This is based on mutational data shown in Figures 1B and 1C.

claim: The internal loop regions (L1) of LINE-1-rbz and OR4K15-rbz are nearly identical except that C8 in OR4K15-rbz is replaced by U38 in LINE-1-rbz.
source: The internal loop regions (L1) of LINE-1-rbz and OR4K15-rbz are nearly identical except that C8 in OR4K15-rbz is replaced by U38 in LINE-1-rbz (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is based on sequence comparison shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The secondary structure of OR4K15-rbz is a circular-permutated version of LINE-1-rbz.
source: Removing the peripheral loop regions (Figure 1B, C) allows us to recognize that the secondary structure of OR4K15-rbz is a circular-permutated version of LINE-1-rbz.
evidence: This is based on structural comparison shown in Figure 3A.

claim: After permutation, OR4K15-rbz has two conserved internal loops with one loop identical to LINE-1-rbz and the other differing by one base.
source: As shown in Figure 3A, after a permutation, OR4K15-rbz has two conserved internal loops with one loop identical to LINE-1-rbz, and the other loop differed from LINE-1-rbz by one base.
evidence: This is based on structural comparison shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The U38C mismatch in L1 has an RA′ of 0.6, suggesting it is not disruptive to the functional structure.
source: The only mismatch U38C in L1 has the RA′ of 0.6, suggesting that the mismatch is not disruptive to the functional structure of the ribozyme.
evidence: This is based on mutational data and inference about structural impact.

claim: Pattern-based similarity search against Rfam database yielded three hits with identical motifs all from the twister sister ribozyme class.
source: We obtained three hits with identical motifs all from the twister sister ribozyme class (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is based on RNAbob search results.

claim: The two internal loops of LINE-1-rbz differ from the catalytic internal loops of the four-way junctional twister sister ribozyme by only one base in each loop.
source: The two internal loops of LINE-1-rbz with 5 and 6 nucleotides, respectively, differ from the catalytic internal loops of the four-way junctional twister sister ribozyme only by one base in each loop (Figure 3A, Zheng et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on sequence comparison shown in Figure 3A and supported by citation.

claim: LINE-1-rbz and OR4K15-rbz are named TS-like ribozymes due to their identical lantern-shaped regions.
source: Given the identical lantern-shaped regions of the LINE-1-rbz and OR4K15-rbz ribozyme, we named them TS-like ribozymes.
evidence: This is a naming decision based on structural similarity.

claim: The homology model of LINE-1-core was built from the four-way junctional twister sister ribozyme (PDB ID: 5Y87).
source: Figure 3B shows the homology-modeled structure of bimolecular LINE-1-core (internal loops plus stems) built from the more identical four-way junctional twister sister ribozyme (PDB ID: 5Y87).
evidence: This is based on homology modeling using the twister sister structure as template.

claim: The LINE-1-core model can be built like the twister sister ribozyme in the internal loops L1, with A11 at the cleavage site directed inwards.
source: Figure 3B, C and Figure 3—figure supplement 2 show that the LINE-1-core model can be built as the twister sister ribozyme in the internal loops L1, with A11 at the cleavage site directed inwards.
evidence: This is based on the homology model shown in the figures.

claim: Stem P1 of LINE-1-rbz is extended by Watson–Crick U9A39 as part of the G7(U9A39) base triple and Watson-Crick C8G40.
source: As shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 3, stem P1 of LINE-1-rbz is extended by the Watson–Crick U9A39 as a part of the G7(U9A39) base triple and Watson-Crick C8G40.
evidence: This is based on the homology model shown in the figures.

claim: Stem P2 of LINE-1-rbz is extended through trans-non-canonical A12G36 and trans sugar edge-Hoogsteen A11C37.
source: Meanwhile, stem P2 of LINE-1-rbz is extended through trans-non-canonical A12G36 and trans sugar edge-Hoogsteen A11C37.
evidence: This is based on the homology model.

claim: G7 in LINE-1-rbz is H-bonded to both non-bridging O atoms of the phosphate connecting C37 and U38.
source: In addition to the triple base interaction in LINE-1-rbz, G7 is also H-bonded to both non-bridging O atoms of the phosphate connecting C37 and U38 (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is based on the homology model shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The H-bond interaction between the proR O atom of the phosphate and A39 N6 generates a stable square array of H-bonds in LINE-1-rbz.
source: This, along with the H-bond interaction between the proR O atom of the phosphate and A39 N6, generates a stable square array of H-bonds.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the homology model.

claim: The model structure of L1 in OR4K15-core is similar to L1 in the LINE-1-core model.
source: As shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4A, B, the model structure of L1 in OR4K15-core is similar to L1 in the LINE-1-core model, with stems P1 and P2 extended by additional base-pairing interactions in the tertiary structure of OR4K15-core.
evidence: This is based on homology modeling shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: The base triple interaction G37(A9U39) exists in OR4K15-core, with G37 H-bonded to A9 N6 rather than U39.
source: The base triple interaction of G37(A9U39) also exists in OR4K15-core, with the difference that G37 is H-bonded to A9 N6, rather than U39 (Figure 3—figure supplement 4C).
evidence: This is based on the homology model shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: The square array of H-bonds is not observed in OR4K15-core because there is no direct interaction between A9 and the phosphate connecting C7 and C8.
source: Thus, the square array of H-bonds could not be observed as there was no direct interaction between A9 and the phosphate connecting C7 and C8.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the OR4K15-core homology model.

claim: The bond between A9 (A39 in LINE-1-core) and the phosphate may not be important, consistent with the fact that replacing the AU pair by a UU pair did not disrupt cleavage activity (RA′ = 0.8 for A39U in LINE-1-rbz).
source: This modeling result suggests that the bond between A9 (A39 in LINE-1-core) and the phosphate may not be important, consistent with the fact that the replacement of the AU pair by a non-canonical UU pair did not disrupt cleavage activity (RA′ = 0.8 for A39U in LINE-1-rbz).

claim: U38 in LINE-1-core (C8 in OR4K15-core) is extruded from the helix like in twister sister ribozyme structures.

claim: In twister sister ribozymes, A8 (three-way junctional) and A7 (four-way junctional) are involved in tertiary contact with stem-loop SL4.

evidence: This is based on previous structural studies of twister sister ribozymes.

claim: The key contacts for U38 of LINE-1-core (C8 in OR4K15-core) are H-bond interaction with A11 N6 (A41 N6 in OR4K15-core) and interactions between the phosphate and G7 (G37 in OR4K15-core).
source: Lacking the extra stem-loops in twister sister ribozyme, the key contacts for U38 of LINE-1-core (C8 in OR4K15-core) are the H-bond interaction with A11 N6 (A41 N6 in OR4K15-core), and the interactions between the phosphate and G7 (G37 in OR4K15-core).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the homology models.

claim: No involvement of the nucleobase part (U38 in LINE-1-core, C8 in OR4K15-core) in the modeled structures is compatible with the mismatches U38C and U38A found in the comparison.
source: No involvement of the nucleobase part (U38 in LINE-1-core, C8 in OR4K15-core) in the modeled structures is compatible with the mismatches U38C and U38A found in the comparison, as changes of the nucleobase part did not have a big influence on the H-bonded interactions involving U38 (C8 in OR4K15-core) (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is an inference based on the homology model and sequence comparison.

claim: It is unclear whether the model structure of TS-like ribozymes built from the twister sister will remain stable in the absence of tertiary interactions with stem-loop SL2.
source: Thus, it is not entirely clear whether the model structure of TS-like ribozymes built from the twister sister will remain stable in the absence of any tertiary interactions with the stem-loop SL2 or it will deviate significantly from the twister sister.
evidence: This is speculation about the validity of the homology model.

claim: Most nucleotides in the L1 region of LINE-1-rbz are relatively conserved, with single mutations showing RA′ < 0.2.
source: Most nucleotides in the L1 region of LINE-1-rbz are relatively conserved, as single mutations showed RA′ < 0.2 according to deep mutational scanning results (Figure 2A).

claim: Mutations of C62 at the cleavage site in twister sister ribozymes did not lead to major changes in cleavage activity.
source: By comparison, mutations of C62 (C54 in three-way junctional twister sister ribozyme) at the cleavage site did not lead to a major change on the cleavage activity in previous studies (Liu et al., 2017; Zheng et al., 2017).

source: As shown in Figure 4C, mutations on C10 showed either partial (C10U, C10G) or complete loss (C10A) in cleavage activity.

claim: C62U and C62A mutations in four-way junctional twister sister ribozyme showed pronounced cleavage activity, while C62G showed somewhat reduced activity.
source: While the corresponding mutations in the four-way junctional twister sister ribozyme showed pronounced (C62U, C62A) or somewhat reduced (C62G) cleavage activity (Liu et al., 2017; Zheng et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on previous studies of twister sister ribozymes.

claim: A11U in LINE-1-core showed partial cleavage activity, whereas A63U in four-way junctional twister sister ribozyme showed complete loss of cleavage activity.
source: More interestingly, A11U in LINE-1-core showed partial cleavage activity, whereas the corresponding mutation A63U in the four-way junctional twister sister ribozyme showed complete loss of cleavage activity (Liu et al., 2017; Zheng et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on experimental data and comparison with previous studies.

claim: Different mutation effects indicate that LINE-1-core may not adopt exactly the same structure and catalytic mechanism as the twister sister ribozyme.
source: These different mutation effects indicate that LINE-1-core may not adopt exactly the same structure and catalytic mechanism as the twister sister ribozyme.
evidence: This is an inference based on the different mutational responses.

claim: TS-like ribozymes may not be simply a minimal version of twister sister ribozymes.
source: In other words, TS-like ribozymes may not be simply a minimal version of twister sister ribozymes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the different mutational responses.

claim: In twister sister ribozymes, nucleotides at the cleavage site (C62-A63 in four-way, C54-A55 in three-way) adopt either a splayed-apart or base-stacked conformation.
source: The corresponding nucleotides in twister sister ribozymes (C62-A63 in four-way junctional twister sister ribozyme, C54-A55 in three-way junctional twister sister ribozyme) adopt either a splayed-apart or a base-stacked conformation, with the scissile phosphate H-bonded to the G5 (four-way junctional twister sister ribozyme) or C7 (three-way junctional twister sister ribozyme).
evidence: This is based on previous structural studies of twister sister ribozymes.

claim: In the modeled structures, the bases at the cleavage site C10-A11 in LINE-1-core (C40-A41 in OR4K15-core) are splayed away, with A11 (A41) directed inwards and C10 (C40) directed outwards.
source: In our modeled structures (Figure 4B, Figure 3—figure supplement 4D), the bases at the cleavage site C10-A11 in LINE-1-core (C40-A41 in OR4K15-core) are splayed away, with A11 (A41 in OR4K15-core) directed inwards and C10 (C40 in OR4K15-core) directed outwards.
evidence: This is based on the homology models shown in the figures.

source: In addition, H-bonded interactions between C10 (C40 in OR4K15-core) and the two nucleotides 3′ of C10 could be found (Figure 4B, Figure 3—figure supplement 4D).
evidence: This is based on the homology models shown in the figures.

claim: Structure differences may partially explain why mutations of C10 were detrimental to catalysis in TS-like ribozymes.
source: These structure differences may partially explain why mutations of C10 were detrimental to the catalysis in TS-like ribozymes.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural analysis and mutational data.

source: Moreover, we did not observe interactions between C10 (C40 in OR4K15-core) and G36/C37 (G6/C7 in OR4K15-core) although they were important to anchor the cytosine in twister sister ribozymes.
evidence: This is based on comparison of the homology models with twister sister structures.

claim: The lack of interactions between C10 and G36/C37 may be due to replacement of the non-canonical pair G5U64 by A12G36 in TS-like ribozymes.
source: This may be due to the replacement of the non-canonical pair G5U64 (G6U57 in three-way junctional twister sister ribozyme) by A12G36 (G6A42 in OR4K15-core) in TS-like ribozymes.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural comparison.

claim: The stability of the current model structure based on the twister sister template is uncertain.
source: Thus, the stability of the current model structure based on the template from the twister sister ribozyme is uncertain.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the structural differences observed.

claim: When the substrate strand was mixed with the enzyme strand, most of the substrate strand was cleaved in the presence of Mg2+.
source: When the substrate strand was mixed with the enzyme strand, most of the substrate strand was cleaved in the presence of Mg2+ (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is based on PAGE cleavage assays shown in Figure 5B.

claim: No cleavage was observed when Mg2+ was not included in the reaction, even after 24 hours of incubation.
source: When Mg2+ was not included in the reaction, no cleavage could be observed even after 24 h's incubation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on PAGE cleavage assays shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: RNA cleavage in TS-like ribozymes is a catalytic reaction accelerated by Mg2+.
source: This result confirms that the RNA cleavage in TS-like ribozymes is a catalytic reaction, accelerated by Mg2+.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the Mg2+ dependence experiments.

claim: The stem-loop SL2 regions in LINE-1-rbz and OR4K15-rbz do not participate in catalytic activity.
source: Moreover, the result confirmed that the stem-loop SL2 regions in LINE-1-rbz and OR4K15-rbz (Figure 2) did not participate in the catalytic activity.
evidence: This is confirmed by the cleavage activity of the core constructs without SL2.

claim: The core constructs of the two TS-like ribozymes contain 35 and 31 nucleotides, respectively, making them the simplest and second simplest self-cleaving ribozymes reported.
source: The core constructs of the two TS-like ribozymes contain 35 and 31 nucleotides, respectively. They are the simplest and the second simplest self-cleaving ribozymes reported so far.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on comparison with other known self-cleaving ribozymes.

claim: Self-cleaving ribozymes cleave through an internal phosphoester transfer mechanism where the 2′-hydroxyl group of the −1 nucleotide attacks the adjacent phosphorus.
source: In all previously reported self-cleaving ribozyme families, the self-cleaving reaction occurs through an internal phosphoester transfer mechanism, in which the 2′-hydroxyl group of the −1 (relative to the cleavage site) nucleotide attacks the adjacent phosphorus resulting in the release of the 5′ oxygen of +1 (relative to the cleavage site) nucleotide (Ferré-D'Amaré and Scott, 2010; Harris et al., 2015; Li et al., 2015; Roth et al., 2014; Weinberg et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge about self-cleaving ribozyme mechanisms supported by citations.

claim: Both LINE-1-core and OR4K15-core employ the same cleavage mechanism as other self-cleaving ribozymes because analogous RNAs lacking the 2′ oxygen atom in the −1 nucleotide were unable to cleave.
source: We confirmed that both LINE-1-core and OR4K15-core employed the same cleavage mechanism because the analogous RNAs that lacked the 2′ oxygen atom in the −1 nucleotide (dC10 for LINE-1-core, dC40 for OR4K15-core) were unable to cleave (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is based on experiments with 2′-deoxy substitutions shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Total loss of cleavage activity in Co(NH3)63+ in the absence of Mg2+ indicates that TS-like ribozymes require binding of divalent cations for both structure folding and catalysis.
source: In Figure 5C and a total loss of cleavage activity in Co(NH3)63+ in the absence of Mg2+ indicates that the TS-like ribozymes require the binding of divalent cations not only for structure folding, but also for catalysis.
evidence: This is based on experiments with Co(NH3)63+ shown in Figure 5C.

claim: At 1 mM concentration, ribozyme cleavage can be observed with Mg2+, Mn2+, Co2+, and Zn2+ but little or none with Ca2+, Cu2+, Ba2+, Ni2+, Na+, K+, Li+, Cs+, or Rb+.
source: At a concentration of 1 mM, ribozyme cleavage can be observed with Mg2+, Mn2+, Co2+, and Zn2+ but little or none with Ca2+, Cu2+, Ba2+, Ni2+, Na+, K+, Li+, Cs+, or Rb+, indicating that direct participation of specific hydrated divalent metal ions is required for self-cleavage.
evidence: This is based on metal ion dependence experiments shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Direct participation of specific hydrated divalent metal ions is required for self-cleavage of TS-like ribozymes.
source: indicating that direct participation of specific hydrated divalent metal ions is required for self-cleavage.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the metal ion dependence experiments.

claim: TS-like ribozymes have equivalent or higher cleavage ratio with Mn2+ than Mg2+.
source: More interestingly, we found that the TS-like ribozymes have an equivalent or even higher cleavage ratio with Mn2+ than Mg2+.
evidence: This is based on metal ion dependence experiments.

claim: For LINE-1-core, the cleaved fractions were ~57% for Mg2+ and ~74% for Mn2+.
source: For LINE-1-core, the cleaved fractions were ~57% for Mg2+, ~74% for Mn2+.
evidence: This is based on quantification of cleavage assays.

claim: For OR4K15-core, the cleaved fractions were ~9% for Mg2+ and ~79% for Mn2+.
source: For OR4K15-core, the cleaved fractions were ~9% for Mg2+, ~79% for Mn2+.
evidence: This is based on quantification of cleavage assays.

claim: The kobs of LINE-1-core under single-turnover condition was ~0.05 min−1 when measured in 10 mM MgCl2 and 100 mM KCl at pH 7.5.
source: The kobs of LINE-1-core under single-turnover condition was ~0.05 min−1 when measured in 10 mM MgCl2 and 100 mM KCl at pH 7.5 (Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is based on kinetic analysis shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: LINE-1-rbz has a kobs of ~0.03 min−1, only slightly lower than LINE-1-core.
source: Only a slightly lower value of kobs (~0.03 min−1) was observed for LINE-1-rbz (Figure 5—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is based on kinetic analysis shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: The stem-loop region SL2 does not contribute much to the cleavage activity of TS-like ribozymes.
source: This confirms that the stem-loop region SL2 does not contribute much to the cleavage activity of the TS-like ribozymes.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on comparison of kobs values for LINE-1-core and LINE-1-rbz.

claim: Cleavage activities of the two TS-like ribozymes are highly dependent on the concentration of divalent metal ions.
source: Cleavage activities of the two TS-like ribozymes were highly dependent on the concentration of divalent metal ions.
evidence: This is based on concentration-dependent kinetic experiments.

claim: The rate constants of two TS-like ribozymes plateau at Mg2+ concentrations above 100 mM.
source: The steep increase in rate constants of two TS-like ribozymes plateaued at Mg2+ concentrations above 100 mM
evidence: This is based on concentration-dependent kinetic experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The rate constants of two TS-like ribozymes plateau at Mn2+ concentrations of 10 mM.
source: while for Mn2+ it plateaued at concentrations of 10 mM.
evidence: This is based on concentration-dependent kinetic experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: LINE-1-core showed higher cleavage rates than OR4K15-core when incubated with Mg2+.
source: Consistent with the PAGE result, LINE-1-core showed higher cleavage rates than OR4K15-core when they were incubated with Mg2+.
evidence: This is based on kinetic analysis.

source: However, the cleavage rates of OR4K15-core were only lower than LINE-1-core when the concentrations of Mn2+ were less than 20 mM, but higher, otherwise.
evidence: This is based on kinetic analysis at different Mn2+ concentrations.

claim: There may exist an important difference between OR4K15-core and LINE-1-core to explain the different bias toward ions.
source: Thus, there may exist an important difference between OR4K15-core and LINE-1-core to explain this different bias toward ions.

source: For OR4K15-rbz, there was an exact match located at the reverse strand of the exon of the OR4K15 gene (Figure 6A).

source: The other three homologs of OR4K15-rbz belong to the same olfactory receptor family 4 subfamily K (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is based on genomic location analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: There is no exact match for LINE-1-rbz in the human genome.

evidence: This is based on genomic location analysis shown in Figure 6A.

evidence: This is based on bioinformatic analysis using RepeatMasker.

claim: Only three LINE-1 subfamilies (L1PA7, L1PA8, and L1P3) can be considered as abundant with LINE-1-rbz homologs (>100 homologs per family).
source: Only three subfamilies L1PA7, L1PA8, and L1P3 (L1PA7-9) can be considered as abundant with LINE-1-rbz homologs (>100 homologs per family).

source: The widespread A12C substitution can be found in the majority of LINE-1-rbz homologs, this substitution leads to a one-base pair extension of the second stem (P2) but almost no activity (RÃ′: 0.03) based on our deep mutational scanning result.

source: For three homologs of OR4K15-rbz, we only found one homolog of OR4K15 with pronounced self-cleavage activity (Figure 6F).

source: Similarly, the majority (15 out of 18) of primate genomes have a large number of LINE-1 homologs (>500) and the remaining three have essentially none.

source: Only one homolog has a single mutation (U38C) in the genome assembly of Gibbon (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).

source: The majority of these homologs have three or more mismatches (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).

source: For OR4K15-rbz, all representative primate genomes contain at least one exact match of the OR4K15-rbz sequence.
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic search in primate genomes.

claim: Most self-cleaving ribozymes are in non-coding regions of the hosting genome.
source: Most self-cleaving ribozymes (Deng et al., 2023) are in non-coding regions of the hosting genome.
evidence: This is a general observation supported by citation.

claim: LINE-1 belongs to the family of retrotransposons and makes up about 17% of the human genome with over 500,000 copies.
source: LINE-1 belongs to the family of retrotransposons, they make up about 17% of the human genome, with over 500,000 copies (Brouha et al., 2003; Lander et al., 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge about LINE-1 elements supported by citations.

claim: The retrotransposition process of LINE-1 increases the copy number of repeats and generates insertional mutations in the genome.
source: The retrotransposition process of LINE-1 increases the copy number of repeats and generates insertional mutations in the genome, which contributes to genetic novelties as well as genomic instability.
evidence: This is established knowledge about LINE-1 retrotransposition.

claim: Known examples of self-cleaving ribozymes in retrotransposons include hammerhead, HDV-like and twister ribozymes.
source: To date the known examples of self-cleaving ribozymes in retrotransposons are the afore-mentioned hammerhead, HDV-like and twister ribozymes.
evidence: This is a summary of known ribozymes in retrotransposons.

claim: HDV-like ribozymes have been found inside the 5′ UTR regions of autonomous retrotransposons including R2, R4, R6, RTEs, SART, Baggins, and L1Tc.
source: Especially, the HDV-like ribozymes have been found inside the 5′ UTR regions of the autonomous retrotransposons, including rDNA-specific (R2, R4, and R6) elements, RTEs (retrotransposon-like elements), telomere-specific SART, Baggins, L1Tc, etc. (Ruminski et al., 2011; Weinberg et al., 2019).
evidence: This is based on previous studies supported by citations.

claim: Retrotransposon-related self-cleaving ribozymes have not been observed in mammalian genomes except for the LINE-1 ribozyme.
source: Interestingly, those retrotransposon-related self-cleaving ribozymes have not been observed in mammalian genomes except for the Long Interspersed Nuclear Element-1 (LINE-1) ribozyme discussed in this study.
evidence: This is an observation about the distribution of ribozymes in mammalian genomes.

claim: Even the LINE-1-rbz sequence has at least two mismatches with ancient human LINE-1 families, which led to loss of self-cleavage activity.
source: However, we found that even this LINE-1-rbz sequence has at least two mismatches with the ancient human LINE-1 families, which led to the loss of self-cleavage activity.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and cleavage assays.

claim: Most TS-like ribozyme homologs found in primate LINE-1 retrotransposons seem to be inactive due to mutations, except for one homolog (U38C) found in Gibbon.
source: Similarly, most TS-like ribozyme homologs found in the primate LINE-1 retrotransposons seem to be inactive due to mutations, except for one homolog (U38C) found in Gibbon.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and activity predictions.

claim: The location of the LINE-1 ribozyme inside the 5′ UTR suggests it might be related to transcriptional regulation of LINE-1 retrotransposon during evolution.
source: Considering the location of the LINE-1 ribozyme inside the 5′ UTR, it suggests that this ribozyme might be related to the transcriptional regulation of the LINE-1 retrotransposon during evolution, like the HDV-like ribozymes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the genomic location and comparison with HDV-like ribozymes.

claim: The majority of LINE-1 retrotransposons inside the genome are 'DNA fossils' that were active in a specific period but became extinct during evolution.
source: Since the majority of the LINE-1 retrotransposons inside the genome are 'DNA fossils' (Beck et al., 2010; Lander et al., 2001), which means that they were active in a specific period but became extinct (dysfunctional) during evolution.
evidence: This is established knowledge about LINE-1 elements supported by citations.

claim: The self-cleavage activity of TS-like ribozymes in LINE-1 retrotransposons may share a common evolutionary path with retrotransposition activity.
source: This suggests that the self-cleavage activity of the TS-like ribozymes in the LINE-1 retrotransposons may share a common evolutionary path with retrotransposition activity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that most LINE-1 elements are inactive.

claim: Antisense transcription is ubiquitous in mammals and may affect gene regulation.
source: suggesting a potentially novel functional mechanism for this ribozyme as antisense transcription is ubiquitous in mammals and may affect the gene regulation (Vivancos et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Progress in understanding the functional roles of LINE-1 and OR4K15 self-cleaving ribozymes was slow because of lacking structural clues.
source: However, the progress in understanding the functional roles of LINE-1 and OR4K15 self-cleaving ribozymes was slow because of lacking structural clues.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field before this study.

claim: The functional regions of both LINE-1 and OR4K15 ribozymes are very short (35 and 31 nucleotides) and in the same class in a circular-permutated form.
source: Indeed, we found that the functional regions for both ribozymes are very short (35 and 31 nucleotides for LINE-1 and OR4K15, respectively) and surprisingly in the same class in a circular-permutated form.
evidence: This is a key finding from the deep mutational scanning experiments.

claim: The consistency between results from deep mutational study of the original sequence and functional region of LINE-1 ribozyme provides confidence about the secondary structures obtained.
source: We are confident about the secondary structures obtained because of the consistency between the results from the deep mutational study of the original sequence and the functional region of the LINE-1 ribozyme.
evidence: This is based on comparison of results from two rounds of deep mutational scanning.

claim: The discovery of functional regions in circular-permutated form from one another further confirms the obtained secondary structure.
source: The obtained secondary structure is further confirmed by the discovery of the functional regions of the two TS-like ribozymes in the circular-permutated form from one another (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The U→C mutation (U38C in LINE-1-rbz, C8U in OR4K15-rbz) shows consistent activity reduction in both ribozymes, confirming they belong to the same class.
source: From the mutational information of LINE-1-rbz, the only mismatch (U38C) from OR4K15 in the catalytic region has an RA′ of 0.6. While the corresponding mismatch mutation C8U in OR4K15 has an RA of 1.54, or 0.65 for U8C. This consistency in activity reduction for the U→C mutation further confirmed that these two ribozymes belong to the same class in a circular-permutated form.
evidence: This is based on mutational data from both ribozymes.

claim: Three classes of self-cleaving ribozymes (hammerhead, twister, and hairpin) are found in different species in multiple circular-permutated forms.
source: Currently, three classes of self-cleaving ribozymes, the hammerhead (de la Peña and García-Robles, 2010b; Jimenez et al., 2011; Przybilski et al., 2005; Seehafer et al., 2011), twister (Roth et al., 2014), and the hairpin (Weinberg et al., 2021) ribozymes are found in different species in multiple circular-permutated forms.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The discovery of permutated TS-like ribozymes in the human genome suggests additional examples of circular-permutated TS-like ribozymes can be found in other species.
source: The discovery of permutated TS-like ribozymes in the human genome for the first time suggests that we can find additional examples of circular-permutated TS-like ribozymes in other species.
evidence: This is speculation based on the discovery and comparison with other ribozyme classes.

claim: The internal loop regions of TS-like ribozymes share high similarity with the catalytic region of twister sister ribozyme (two mismatches only).
source: More interestingly, we found that the internal loop regions of the TS-like ribozymes share a high similarity with the known catalytic region of the twister sister ribozyme (two mismatches only, Figure 3A).
evidence: This is based on sequence comparison shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The conserved cleavage sites suggest a similar structure and mechanism between TS-like and twister sister ribozymes.
source: The conserved cleavage sites suggest a similar structure and mechanism as shown in Figure 3A.
evidence: This is an inference based on sequence similarity.

claim: The maximum observed rate constant (kobs) for twister sister ribozyme is ~5 min−1, compared to ~0.11 ± 0.01 min−1 for TS-like ribozymes.
source: However, the maximum observed rate constant (kobs) for the twister sister ribozyme was ~5 min−1 (Weinberg et al., 2015), compared to ~0.11 ± 0.01 min−1 for the TS-like ribozymes.
evidence: This is based on kinetic measurements and comparison with previous studies.

claim: The rate difference between twister sister and TS-like ribozymes is not mainly caused by mismatches in the catalytic core.
source: This rate difference is not mainly caused by mismatches in the catalytic core between the twister sister and LINE-1/OR4K15 ribozymes.
